title: How unique is a browser fingerprint?
hook: Studies of volunteers found up to 89% unique. A study of ordinary visitors found 34%.
collected: Browser and device attributes any site can read (see the Mirror Room).
inferred: Whether a browser can be recognised again without cookies.
done: Eckersley (EFF, 2010) found 83.6% of 470,161 browsers unique; Laperdrix et al. (IEEE S&P 2016) found 89.4% of 118,934. Both used volunteers on privacy-test sites. Gómez-Boix et al. (The Web Conference 2018) studied 2,067,942 fingerprints from a general French website and found only 33.6% unique.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: Peer-reviewed measurements. The difference is about WHO was measured.

outcome.text: Browsers (Safari, Firefox, Brave) have since reduced some exposed details.

sources.title: How Unique Is Your Web Browser?
Beauty and the Beast: Diverting modern web browsers to build unique browser fingerprints
Hiding in the Crowd: an Analysis of the Effectiveness of Browser Fingerprinting at Large Scale

whyItMatters: How strong a finding is depends on who was in the sample.

title: A crawl of the top 1 million websites for tracking
hook: Canvas fingerprinting scripts were found on 14,371 sites.
collected: Canvas, audio and font fingerprints, local network addresses and more.
inferred: A device identity that survives cookie clearing.
done: Englehardt and Narayanan (ACM CCS 2016) found canvas fingerprinting on 14,371 sites (from about 400 script domains), canvas-based font detection on 3,250, audio fingerprinting on 67 and WebRTC local-IP discovery on 715. The Battery API was used by only about two scripts.
label: DOCUMENTED
whyItMatters: The demo in the Mirror Room uses the same techniques found on real sites.

title: The battery level that became a tracking ID
hook: A precise battery reading could link your visits for a few minutes. Firefox removed the feature.
collected: Battery level and charge or discharge time.
howObtained: The HTML5 Battery Status API, readable by any page.
inferred: A short-lived identifier, because the precise reading was unusual.
done: Olejnik, Acar, Castelluccia and Diaz (2015) showed the readings were precise enough to act as a short-term tracking ID across sites.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: Peer-reviewed privacy analysis; browser changes are documented in their release notes.

companyResponse.text: Firefox removed the API from web pages in version 52 (2017); Safari never shipped it; Chrome still supports it.

outcome.text: Removed in Firefox; never in Safari; still in Chromium browsers.

sources.title: The leaking battery: A privacy analysis of the HTML5 Battery Status API

limits: Mostly historical; rarely used by trackers (about two scripts in a 2016 crawl).
whyItMatters: A harmless-looking feature became a privacy risk and was removed. Battery is also the subject of a pricing myth.

title: Session replay scripts recorded everything you typed
hook: Some sites let third parties watch your visit like a video, including card numbers.
collected: Mouse movements, clicks, scrolling and keystrokes, sometimes before you press 'submit'.
howObtained: Third-party 'session replay' scripts embedded by websites.
inferred: Where users struggle or hesitate; personal data on the page.
done: Princeton researchers found replay scripts from 7 vendors on 482 of the top 50,000 sites (a lower bound). They observed a full card number and CVV sent to a replay vendor on one retailer's site and a prescription name on another.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: Reproducible technical analysis by university researchers (blog report, not peer-reviewed).

outcome.text: Some sites and vendors changed settings after disclosure.

sources.title: No boundaries: Exfiltration of personal data by session-replay scripts

whyItMatters: You can watch a harmless version of this in the Mirror Room.

title: Panoptispy: no secret microphone recording found, but secret screen recording
hook: 17,260 Android apps were tested for covert audio. None found. Some recorded the screen.
collected: Tested for: audio, images, video and screenshots leaving apps.
howObtained: Static and dynamic analysis of apps.
done: Pan, Ren, Lindorfer, Wilson and Choffnes (PETS 2018) analysed 17,260 apps and found no evidence of covert microphone exfiltration, but found third-party libraries recording and uploading screen video and screenshots without telling users.
label: DOCUMENTED

companyResponse.text: One affected app removed the screen-recording SDK after disclosure.

sources.title: Panoptispy: Characterizing Audio and Video Exfiltration from Android Applications
Android apps can slurp your screen

limits: Android, 2017-era apps. Absence of evidence in a big sample is strong but not total.
whyItMatters: The real surprise wasn't the microphone. It was the screen.

title: InMobi inferred location from Wi-Fi even when users said no
hook: Deny location permission, and the nearby Wi-Fi network names can still give it away.
inferred: Location, by matching Wi-Fi networks against a database.
done: The FTC alleged InMobi tracked consumers' locations, including those who had denied location permission, and collected children's data.
affected: Users of apps carrying the SDK.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: FTC settlement. No admission of wrongdoing.

outcome.text: $4 million penalty (suspended to $950,000 based on ability to pay).

sources.title: Mobile Advertising Network InMobi Settles FTC Charges

limits: Operating systems have since restricted Wi-Fi scanning.
whyItMatters: 'No' to one permission doesn't always mean no.

title: Ultrasonic beacons: TV ads that talk to your phone
hook: Inaudible tones in ads or shops could tell an app where you were.
collected: Inaudible audio tones picked up by a phone microphone.
howObtained: Code from SilverPush and others in apps with microphone permission.
inferred: Which ad you saw or which shop you entered, linking devices.
done: The FTC warned 12 app developers in March 2016 about SilverPush code. Arp et al. (IEEE EuroS&P 2017) found 234 app samples containing SilverPush code and beacons in 4 of 35 shops tested.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: FTC warning letters (advisory, not enforcement) and peer-reviewed measurement.

sources.title: FTC Issues Warning Letters to App Developers Using 'Silverpush' Code
Privacy Threats through Ultrasonic Side Channels on Mobile Devices

limits: Requires microphone permission. Uptake appears limited.
whyItMatters: The real microphone story is more specific, and odder, than 'it listens to conversations'.
